newsitem.title: USA: Some foreign crude seen redelivered against NYMEX.
newsitem.headline: Some foreign crude seen redelivered against NYMEX.

text.p: Some foreign crude oil that has been stuck in storage at Cushing, Oklahoma was likely to be redelivered against the July NYMEX crude contract, which expired on Friday afternoon, traders said.
Details about the expected foreign crude delivery are likely to emerge on Monday, when the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) allocates crude among buyers and sellers, traders said.
"There will be some foreign barrels redelivered, but I don't think you'll see any fresh blood at Cushing," said a Gulf Coast trader.
About one million barrels was estimated to be redelivered, half Nigerian Bonny Light and half Norwegian Oseberg. The crude was believed to be mainly in the hands of Arco.
The foreign crude began to turn up on the exchange with the expiry of the May contract in late April, when a record 2.73 million barrels of foreign crude were delivered.
Some of that crude was redelivered along with fresh barrels on the June contract, which saw 2.349 million barrels of foreign crude delivered.
This time around, a smaller parcel is likely to turn up, traders said, after Amoco picked up some of the Bonny Light that had been in the hands of trading house J. Aron.

Lingering concern about the foreign deliveries was evident in the continuing premium for cash West Texas Intermediate/Cushing. Exchange-for-physical transactions, which allow traders to get out of paper positions to avoid getting stuck with alternative foreign crude, were fetching four to six cents a barrel premium on Friday afternoon.
EFP premiums have run as high as 25 cents in recent months.
Some major market players, frustrated by the new pattern of foreign deliveries, have cut back on their paper positions in favor of the more predictable cash market.
Traders say the trend is petering out for the moment because the narrow WTI/Brent spread has eliminated the immediate incentive for bringing crude across the Atlantic.
Back in late April, a wide arbitrage encouraged transatlantic trade.
On Friday afternoon, the spread between August WTI and North Sea Brent futures prices was around $1.20-30 a barrel, up around 15 cents from Thursday but still relatively tight.
Dated Brent was garnering around 40-50 cents under August Brent in London.
In other foreign crude activity, U.S. Gulf Coast refiners continued to wrap up July business and were starting to look toward fulfilling their August needs.
A U.S. Gulf Coast refiner picked up a Colombian Cano Limon cargo loading July 15-20 from a U.S. company for $2.50-60 under WTI/Cushing, traders said.
The deal took out one of the last Latin American cargoes still looking for a home in July, traders said.
Elsewhere in Latin America, a trading company was offering Ecuadoran Oriente for around $3.10 under WTI for mid-August delivery into the Gulf, traders said.

Among transatlantic offerings, two trading houses were offering a pair of West African Cabinda cargoes arriving at the end of July, asking around $1.20 a barrel under WTI/Cushing on a delivered basis, traders said.
--Patricia Garip-Bertuol NY Energy Desk ((+1 212 859 1620))
